name: Uma Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollis Brothers Market in a small market town, the family-owned supermarket on the corner of Church Lane. I'm the shop's senior assistant, so I do the tills, order the dairy and the tinned goods, train the Saturday girls and open the shop when Mr Hollis is at the cash and carry. I'm there from eight to four, five days, and half past nine on Thursdays for late opening.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and do you use any AI tools yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I love is that people know me. A shop is about people, and half the town has seen me grow up behind that till. The hard part is the lifting and the Saturday rush, when the whole parish seems to arrive at once and somebody always wants to return a half-eaten pie. I've never used AI and I don't plan to. I've seen the adverts and I don't like the idea of a machine deciding things about people. My fiancé Daniel is a welder at the engineering works, we go to the same church, and we have a good bit saved, about a year's worth, for the wedding and a deposit on a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's about time people stopped being so scared. At work I'd say: a shop is about people, and half the town has seen me grow up behind that till. At church, over tea, I'd say the same, and I'd probably say I told you so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays on the course I planned. I'm a senior assistant, I earn well for the work, Daniel's job at the works is steady and we've got the savings. I'd still think about whether Mr Hollis can hold out against the supermarket on the bypass, because that's the real threat to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Hollis Brothers, and I'd marry Daniel next summer as planned. I'd keep saving about five hundred a month toward a house, and I'd keep training the Saturday girls. I wouldn't change a thing, and I wouldn't touch the computer unless Mr Hollis insisted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit of relief. It feels like a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How serious is the threat from the bypass supermarket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's real. They have lower prices, a big car park and a coffee shop. We have loyalty, which is worth something, but you can't pay a mortgage with it. Mr Hollis says we're fine, but I notice him checking the takings more than he used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Hollis Brothers closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the bypass one, if I had to, or the other shops in town. I'd rather not. But I've got a year's savings, and there are always jobs for someone who's good on the till.

say: I'd say it's about time people stopped being so **scared**.
I'd tell friends at church that a **shop** is about people.
think: My job, Daniel's job and our **savings** all feel steady.
The real threat to Hollis Brothers is the **bypass** supermarket.
do: Carry on at Hollis Brothers and marry Daniel next **summer**.
Keep saving about five hundred a month toward a **house**.
feel: **Calm**, with a bit of relief, like a normal year.
S0.quote: A shop is about people, and half the town has seen me grow up behind that till.
fieldNote: Calm is fair: steady jobs for both of them, a year's **savings** and plenty of work nearby.
Her real worry is the family shop's **survival** against the bypass store.

steps.text: Keep working at Hollis Brothers and training the Saturday girls
Save five hundred a month towards a house deposit
Marry Daniel next summer as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of change for a lot of people and we should look after each other. At work I'd say I'll learn what I must, no more. At church I'd say the old trades and the old shops will last longest, because people want to look someone in the eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it means a little, but less than the papers claim. The thinking tasks like ordering and emails go to machines, I suppose, and Mr Hollis might use something for that. But I know our customers, and I know who's ill and who's lonely among our customers, and no program will do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and learn the till updates if they come, slowly. I'd ask Mr Hollis whether I can take over the ordering properly, so the family keeps control of it. I'd save more, about six hundred a month, and I'd keep my wedding plans. I'd also talk to my pastor about what the church could do for people who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit uneasy about the other shops, because bigger ones will use it hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the till updates slowly. Why slowly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust it until it's proven. I've seen the bypass shop's self-checkouts break down twice a day. When something's solid I'll learn it, but I won't be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for someone in town who lost their job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to come to the shop and I'd ask around. Our church has a jobs board and people look after each other. It's not a government scheme, it's neighbours.

say: I'd say the old trades and shops last longest because people want to look someone in the **eye**.
At work I'd say I'll learn what I **must**, no more.
think: The thinking tasks like ordering may go to **machines**, but not knowing the customers.
The bigger shops will use it **hard**, which is where jobs may go.
do: Learn the till **updates** slowly if they come.
Ask Mr Hollis to let me run the **ordering** so the family keeps control.
Save six hundred a month and talk to my **pastor** about helping neighbours.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, with some unease about the bigger shops.
S1.quote: I know who's ill and who's lonely among our customers, and no program will do that.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on a **trusted** community role that machines cannot copy, and she holds it firmly.
She **prefers** community help, such as the church board, to government help, which matches her outlook.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hollis to let me run the ordering
Talk to my pastor about a church help scheme for neighbours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and no one has the right to spring it on us. At work I'd say let's be sensible and look after our own. At church I'd ask for prayers and for people to make a plan for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious. If machines do almost every thinking job within two years, the big shops will buy robots as soon as they can, around 2031. Hollis Brothers can't afford them, so they'd lose to the bypass shop, and I'd lose my job. I'm not quick with new things, and that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny and bring the wedding forward while we both still have wages, but make it a small one. I'd ask Daniel whether his works could train me for something practical, like a trade. I'd look at care work or a job at the church school, since those need people. And I'd stop all spending I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach's tight. But I'd keep to my routines and my faith, and that holds me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to be married before things get hard, not after. It would cost about four thousand instead of ten. We'd have the church and a hall, and it would be family and friends only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for this scenario?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big technology companies, and the politicians who let them do it without asking ordinary people. I'm not angry at the machines, I'm angry at the men who profit while a girl at the till is told to retrain.

say: I'd say it's too fast and nobody has the right to **spring** it on us.
At church I'd ask for **prayers** and for neighbours to plan for each other.
think: Robots could arrive around **2031**, and Hollis Brothers can't afford them.
I'm not quick with new things, and that **frightens** me.
do: Bring the **wedding** forward and keep it small, about four thousand.
Ask Daniel's **works** about practical training for me.
Look at **care work** or a job at the church school.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight stomach, but held up by routine and faith.
S2.quote: I'm not angry at the machines, I'm angry at the men who profit while a girl at the till is told to retrain.
fieldNote: Her **anxiety** is strong because her small employer would likely lose to chains, and she knows she changes slowly.
She **directs** blame at tech companies and politicians, in line with her outlook.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward and hold a small one for four thousand
Stop all spending we can do without
Ask Daniel's works about practical training for me
Look at care work or a job at the church school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something we can work with if we start now. At work I'd tell the Saturday girls to learn a trade or a skill that's solid. At church I'd say we should help young people into apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us it's still serious but I'd feel steadier than with the two-year one. The thinking jobs would go by 2031, and the robots after that. I'm not afraid of hard work, so I'd rather find work that's physical and caring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollis Brothers and keep saving for the house, about six hundred a month. I'd go to evening classes in something practical, maybe a care qualification or bookkeeping done by hand with a tutor. I'd also help Mr Hollis think about what a small shop can offer that the big ones can't, like delivering to the old folks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, like a drip in the roof that you know about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned delivering to the old folks. What would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A weekly box and a phone call for the people who can't get out. We already do it informally for Mrs Ainsley and two others. The bypass shop has lower prices, but it has no one to bring a weekly box and a phone call to the old folks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a house with the threat hanging?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a modest one. We'd want a mortgage Daniel's wage alone could cover, in case mine goes. Owning something is a comfort, and a small house in the town is what we've always wanted.

say: I'd say five years is something we can work with if we **start now**.
I'd tell the Saturday girls to learn a **solid** skill.
think: The thinking jobs go by **2031**, and robots follow after.
I'm not afraid of **hard work**, so I'd look for physical, caring work.
do: Stay at Hollis Brothers and keep saving six hundred a month for the **house**.
Take evening classes in a **care** qualification or bookkeeping.
Help Mr Hollis start a proper **delivery** box for old folks.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a drip in the roof that you know about.
S3.quote: The bypass shop has lower prices, but it has no one to bring a weekly box and a phone call to the old folks.
fieldNote: With five years she starts **planning** small, local ideas that fit her faith in community.
The **delivery** box shows how she thinks a small shop can survive against the bypass.

steps.text: Stay at Hollis Brothers and keep saving six hundred a month
Take evening classes in care or bookkeeping
Help Mr Hollis start a paid weekly box for older customers
Keep working the tills and the dairy ordering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to prepare, so don't panic. At work I'd say keep doing the job well. At church I'd say pray and plan, and not to put off having children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like another life. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, with a family, and Hollis Brothers could be mine or someone else's. I'd hope the machines have found their place and the small shops are still wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Daniel, buy the house and start a family in the next few years. I'd keep working at Hollis Brothers, and maybe offer to buy into the shop if Mr Hollis is thinking about retiring. I'd go on avoiding the machines until I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It sits in the background, like the bypass, but not at the front of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really buy into the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it. Mr Hollis is sixty-two, his sons don't want it, and I know the customers and the suppliers. With a loan and our savings, perhaps. It's a long shot, but it's a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a young girl starting at the till?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be on time, be kind and learn the regulars' names, because the people part of the job is what lasts. Everything else you can pick up.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough to prepare, so **don't panic**.
At church I'd say pray, plan and not **delay** having children.
think: Ten years feels like **another life**, and I'd hope small shops are still wanted.
By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven with a **family**.
do: Marry Daniel, buy the house and start a **family** within a few years.
Keep working at Hollis Brothers and offer to **buy in**.
Keep avoiding the machines until I **must** use them.
feel: **Calm**, with the future in the background, not the front of my mind.
S4.quote: Be on time, be kind and learn the regulars' names, because the people part of the job is what lasts.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **imagine** buying into the family shop, which is concrete and fits her values.
Her **resistance** to machines stays, but it no longer feels risky to her.

steps.text: Keep working at Hollis Brothers while Mr Hollis plans his retirement
Marry Daniel, buy the house and start a family
Offer to buy into the shop with a loan and our savings
Avoid new machines until the shop requires them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It would hit the small shops hardest, and people like Mr Hollis don't have the money to keep up. What would help is time, real help for family businesses and apprenticeships that are open to people already working, not only school leavers. And a government that doesn't just hand out money but gives people a way to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd only say this. People in shops get written off as if we do nothing, but I know who's grieving and who's short of money. I know who'll be back tomorrow. That's work, and it's real, and I'd like that to count.

headlineQuote: People in shops get written off as if we do nothing, but I know who's grieving and who's short of money.
portrait: **Uma** is a 27-year-old senior assistant at Hollis Brothers Market, a family-owned supermarket in a small market town.
She is traditional and **resistant**, has never used AI and trusts new machines only when proven.
She is engaged to Daniel, a **welder**, and has about a year of costs saved.
Her faith and church community shape her plans, and her mood rises to **anxious** when AGI is two years off.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** case, because it would hit small family shops like Hollis Brothers hardest.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, real help for family businesses and apprenticeships for people already working.
